## Organisation of the study

In line with our research question, we use empirical and simulated multinomial data and will use different Random Forests implementations to classify this data. Since our goal is to compare different R packages, we will consider different goodness of fit measures after classification and evaluate the performance of the R packages in this way.

## Preparing the data

For our analysis, we use empirical data on the one hand. The data set originally stems from (...) and contains data on cover tree types. In forestry, a cover tree type is determined by the most prevalent tree type in a certain forest area (REFERENCE). Since the data set contains not only a large amount of observations but also many predictors, it is suitable for the use in our study.
On the other hand, we simulated data for which we also aimed at getting a large number of observations and predictors.
In the following, we describe the simulation of the second data set we use in the analysis. Randomly, we draw from different (WHICH?) distributions to get artificial multinomial data and predictor variables. The simulated multinomial data then consists of (HOW MANY) different tree types, on the one hand. On the other hand, we arrive at a large number of predictors. Moreover, we included correlations between the predictors in the simulation process as we would find these in an empirical data set.(HOW DID WE INCLUDE THE CORRELATIONS)

## The different packages
1. randomForest:
Classification and regression based on a forest of trees using random inputs, based on Breiman (2001).
2. ranger:
A fast implementation of Random Forests, particularly suited for high dimensional data. Ensembles of classification, regression, survival and probability prediction trees are supported. 
3. caret:
Misc. functions for training and plotting classification and regression models.
